questions.explanation: Brown algal oogamous species may fuse gametes in water or inside oogonium.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A marine alga with 2 unequal, laterally attached flagella, laminarin as reserve food and algin in the cell wall belongs to:
questions.explanation: These are defining traits of Phaeophyceae (brown algae) in Table 3.1.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches algal class with its cell wall composition (Table 3.1)?
questions.option_c: Rhodophyceae — cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters
questions.explanation: Rhodophyceae cell walls contain cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Green algae (Chlorophyceae) according to Table 3.1 possess flagella that are:
questions.explanation: Chlorophyceae have 2–8 equal, apically inserted flagella.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which algal class is characterised by chlorophyll a, d and phycoerythrin as major pigments?
questions.explanation: Rhodophyceae (red algae) have chlorophyll a, d and phycoerythrin.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Mannitol and laminarin as stored food are characteristic of which division of algae?
questions.explanation: Phaeophyceae store food as mannitol and laminarin.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Among the three algal classes in Table 3.1, fresh water habitat is LEAST typical for:
questions.option_d: All occur equally in fresh water
questions.explanation: Phaeophyceae occur in fresh water only rarely; they are primarily marine.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pear-shaped zoospores with two unequal laterally attached flagella are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Brown algae produce biflagellate, pear-shaped zoospores with unequal lateral flagella.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The outer layer of the cell wall in green algae is composed of:
questions.explanation: Chlorophyceae cell wall: inner cellulose, outer pectose.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pyrenoids in green algae are associated with storage of:
questions.explanation: Pyrenoids in chloroplasts contain protein besides starch.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In kelps (brown algae), the photosynthetic leaf-like structure is the:
questions.explanation: Brown algal body: holdfast, stipe and frond (photosynthetic).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Bryophytes are called 'amphibians of plant kingdom' because they:
questions.option_a: Complete their life cycle only in water
questions.option_b: Live on land but need water for sexual reproduction
questions.option_c: Have vascular tissue like amphibians have dual circulation
questions.explanation: Bryophytes are terrestrial for growth but water-dependent for fertilisation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In the bryophyte life cycle, the multicellular dominant phase is:
questions.explanation: Bryophytes show gametophytic dominance; main plant body is haploid gametophyte.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The shift from gametophytic dominance (bryophytes) to sporophytic dominance occurs in:
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes are the first group where sporophyte is dominant and differentiated.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In bryophytes, the sporophyte is nutritionally dependent on gametophyte because sporophyte is:
questions.option_b: Parasitic or partially dependent on gametophyte
questions.explanation: Bryophyte sporophyte remains attached and derives nourishment from gametophyte.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pteridophytes differ from bryophytes primarily because pteridophytes possess:
questions.option_b: True roots, stems, leaves with vascular tissue
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes have vascular xylem/phloem and differentiated sporophyte organs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Both bryophytes and pteridophytes require water for fertilisation because:
questions.option_b: Antherozoids must swim to reach the archegonium
questions.explanation: Flagellated antherozoids swim in water to archegonium in both groups.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In moss life cycle, the filamentous protonema develops directly from:
questions.explanation: Moss protonema arises directly from germination of haploid spore.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes liverwort and moss sporophytes?
questions.option_a: Liverwort sporophyte is more elaborate than moss sporophyte
questions.option_b: Both lack foot, seta and capsule
questions.option_c: Moss sporophyte is more elaborate with better spore dispersal
questions.explanation: Moss sporophyte is more elaborate than liverwort sporophyte.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A pteridophyte producing only one type of spore is termed:
questions.explanation: Majority of pteridophytes are homosporous (one spore type).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Heterospory in pteridophytes is shown by:
questions.explanation: Selaginella and Salvinia produce macro- and microspores (heterosporous).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Selaginella belongs to class Lycopsida. Equisetum belongs to:
questions.explanation: Equisetum (horsetail) is in Sphenopsida; Selaginella is Lycopsida.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Microphylls with a single unbranched vascular strand are found in:
questions.explanation: Selaginella has small microphylls; ferns have large macrophylls.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The most fundamental distinction between gymnosperms and angiosperms is:
questions.option_b: Angiosperms enclose ovules in ovary; gymnosperms have naked ovules
questions.option_c: Gymnosperms are always herbs; angiosperms are always trees
questions.explanation: Angiosperms have ovules in ovary and seeds in fruits; gymnosperms have naked ovules/seeds.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which statement about gametophytes in gymnosperms is CORRECT?
questions.option_a: Both male and female gametophytes are free-living
questions.option_b: Male gametophyte is pollen grain; female gametophyte retained in ovule
questions.option_c: Female gametophyte is called prothallus and grows independently
questions.option_d: Gametophyte is the dominant plant body
questions.explanation: Gymnosperm gametophytes are retained within sporangia/ovule, not free-living.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Coralloid roots associated with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are found in:
questions.explanation: Cycas has coralloid roots with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria; Pinus has mycorrhiza.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Fertilisation in gymnosperms differs from pteridophytes because gymnosperms use:
questions.option_b: Pollen grains and pollen tube to deliver male gametes
questions.explanation: Gymnosperms use airborne pollen; pollen tube delivers gametes to archegonia in ovule.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: After fertilisation in angiosperms, the ovule develops into seed and ovary develops into:
questions.explanation: Angiosperm seeds are enclosed in fruit formed from ovary.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Wolffia and Eucalyptus cited in the chapter illustrate angiosperm diversity in:
questions.explanation: Wolffia is among smallest angiosperms; Eucalyptus exceeds 100 m in height.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In pteridophytes, meiosis occurs during formation of spores in:
questions.explanation: Spore mother cells in sporangia of sporophyte undergo meiosis in pteridophytes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Prothallus cell of a fern is:
questions.explanation: Prothallus is the haploid gametophyte of pteridophytes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Zygote of a fern immediately after fertilisation is:
questions.explanation: Zygote forms by fusion of haploid gametes, hence is diploid (2n).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Microsporangiate strobili in gymnosperms are also called:
questions.explanation: Strobili with microsporophylls/microsporangia are male (microsporangiate) cones.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Spiral ribbon-shaped chloroplast is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Spirogyra (Chlorophyceae) has distinctive spiral ribbon chloroplasts.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sargassum and Laminaria are economically important as:
questions.option_a: Sources of agar for microbial culture
questions.option_b: Marine brown algae used as food
questions.explanation: Sargassum and Laminaria are marine brown algae used as food.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Numerical taxonomy (phenetics) differs from artificial systems because it:
questions.option_b: Assigns equal weight to hundreds of observable characters
questions.option_d: Is based solely on habit and leaf colour
questions.explanation: Numerical taxonomy codes all observable characters and gives them equal weight.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Compact strobili formed by sporophylls occur in:
questions.explanation: Selaginella and Equisetum form strobili/cones from sporophylls.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In gymnosperms, nucellus surrounded by protective envelopes constitutes:
questions.explanation: Ovule = nucellus + protective envelopes; megasporophyll bears ovules.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Needle-like leaves with thick cuticle and sunken stomata in conifers are adaptations for:
questions.explanation: Reduced surface area, thick cuticle and sunken stomata minimise transpiration.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sequoia (giant redwood) exemplifies gymnosperms as:
questions.explanation: Sequoia is a gymnosperm and among the tallest trees.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Large pinnately compound leaves persisting for few years are seen in:
questions.explanation: Cycas has pinnate leaves that persist for a few years.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ecological role of algae in aquatic ecosystems includes:
questions.option_b: Acting as primary producers and increasing dissolved oxygen
questions.explanation: Photosynthetic algae fix CO₂ and raise dissolved O₂; they are primary producers.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Anisogamous reproduction in algae is exemplified by:
questions.explanation: Eudorina shows anisogamy — fusion of dissimilar-sized gametes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Basis of classification of algae into three classes includes:
questions.option_b: Type of pigments and stored food
questions.explanation: Algae are classified by pigments possessed and type of stored food.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Oogamous sexual reproduction occurs in Volvox and Fucus. In oogamy:
questions.option_a: Both gametes are flagellated and equal in size
questions.option_b: Female gamete is small and motile; male gamete is large and static
questions.option_c: Female gamete is large, non-motile; male gamete is smaller and motile
questions.option_d: Gametes are non-motile and of equal size
questions.explanation: Oogamy = large static female + smaller motile male gamete.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Why is classification of animals important according to NCERT?
questions.option_a: To reduce the number of animal species
questions.option_b: To assign systematic position to newly described species
questions.option_c: To eliminate extinct species from records
questions.option_d: To merge similar phyla into one group
questions.explanation: Classification helps assign a systematic position to newly described species among over a million described animal species.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which level of organisation is exhibited by sponges?
questions.explanation: Sponges show cellular level of organisation with cells arranged as loose aggregates.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Coelenterates exhibit which level of body organisation?
questions.explanation: In coelenterates, cells performing the same function are arranged into tissues (tissue level).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Organ level of organisation is first seen in which phylum among the following?
questions.explanation: Platyhelminthes and higher phyla exhibit organ level where tissues form organs specialised for particular functions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Organ system level of organisation is seen in:
questions.option_c: Annelids, Arthropods, Molluscs, Echinoderms and Chordates
questions.explanation: Annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates show organ system level organisation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: An incomplete digestive system has:
questions.option_b: A single opening serving as both mouth and anus
questions.option_d: Multiple openings along the body wall
questions.explanation: Incomplete digestive system has one opening that functions as both mouth and anus, as in Platyhelminthes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A complete digestive system is characterised by:
questions.option_b: Mouth and anus as two separate openings
questions.explanation: Complete digestive systems possess two openings: mouth and anus.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In an open circulatory system:
questions.option_a: Blood flows only through closed vessels
questions.option_b: Blood is pumped out of the heart and directly bathes cells and tissues
questions.option_d: Blood circulates only in gill capillaries
questions.explanation: Open circulation: blood leaves the heart and bathes tissues directly rather than staying confined to vessels.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Closed circulatory system is characterised by:
questions.option_a: Blood bathing tissues directly without vessels
questions.option_b: Blood circulating through arteries, veins and capillaries
questions.option_d: Blood flowing only in the coelomic cavity
questions.explanation: In closed circulation, blood moves through a network of vessels of varying diameters.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sponges typically show:
questions.explanation: Sponges are mostly asymmetrical; no plane through the centre divides them into equal halves.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Radial symmetry means the body can be divided into identical halves by:
questions.option_b: Any plane through the central axis
questions.explanation: Radial symmetry: any plane through the central axis produces two identical halves.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which group exhibits radial symmetry (in adults)?
questions.explanation: Coelenterates, ctenophores and adult echinoderms show radial symmetry.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Bilateral symmetry is shown by:
questions.explanation: Annelids, arthropods and similar animals show bilateral symmetry (one plane divides into left and right halves).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Diploblastic animals have:
questions.option_c: Mesoderm only between gut and body wall
questions.explanation: Diploblastic animals possess two germ layers: ectoderm and endoderm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Mesoglea is found between:
questions.option_a: Ectoderm and endoderm in diploblastic animals
questions.option_b: Mesoderm and endoderm in triploblastic animals
questions.option_c: Body wall and coelom in annelids
questions.explanation: Mesoglea is the undifferentiated jelly-like layer between ectoderm and endoderm in diploblastic animals.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Triploblastic organisation is seen from which phylum onwards?
questions.explanation: Triploblastic animals (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) range from platyhelminthes to chordates.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Coelom is defined as a body cavity:
questions.option_d: Filled with pseudocoelomic fluid only in annelids
questions.explanation: True coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which of the following is a coelomate?
questions.explanation: Annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates are coelomates.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pseudocoelomates include:
questions.explanation: Aschelminths possess a pseudocoelom — body cavity not lined by mesoderm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Acoelomates are exemplified by:
questions.explanation: Platyhelminthes lack a body cavity and are acoelomates.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Metamerism (metameric segmentation) is well seen in:
questions.explanation: Earthworm body shows metameric segmentation (metamerism) with serial repetition of organs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Notochord is:
questions.explanation: Notochord is a mesodermally derived rod-like structure on the dorsal side during embryonic development.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Non-chordates include phyla from:
questions.explanation: Non-chordates range from Porifera to Echinodermata; chordates possess a notochord.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Members of phylum Porifera are commonly called:
questions.explanation: Porifera members are commonly known as sponges.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Porifera are generally:
questions.explanation: Sponges are generally marine and mostly asymmetrical.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Porifera exhibit which level of organisation?
questions.explanation: Porifera are primitive multicellular animals with cellular level of organisation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Water exits the sponge body through:
questions.explanation: Water enters via ostia into spongocoel and leaves through the osculum.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Choanocytes in sponges are also called:
questions.explanation: Choanocytes (collar cells) line the spongocoel and canals.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Digestion in sponges is:
questions.explanation: Sponges carry out intracellular digestion.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sponge skeleton may consist of:
questions.explanation: Sponge body is supported by spicules or spongin fibres.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sponges are:
questions.explanation: Sponges are hermaphrodite; same individual produces eggs and sperms.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sponge development is:
questions.option_b: Indirect with a distinct larval stage
questions.explanation: Sponges show internal fertilisation and indirect development with a morphologically distinct larva.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Spongilla is a:
questions.explanation: Spongilla is the freshwater sponge example in NCERT.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Euspongia is commonly known as:
questions.explanation: Euspongia is the bath sponge.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The water transport system in sponges helps in:
questions.option_a: Food gathering, respiratory exchange and waste removal
questions.explanation: Water canal system aids food gathering, gas exchange and waste removal.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Coelenterates are:
questions.explanation: Coelenterates are aquatic (mostly marine), sessile or free-swimming, radially symmetrical.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Cnidoblasts contain:
questions.explanation: Cnidoblasts/cnidocytes bear nematocysts (stinging capsules); name Cnidaria reflects this.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Nematocysts are used for:
questions.explanation: Cnidoblasts with nematocysts aid anchorage, defence and prey capture.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Cnidarians are:
questions.explanation: Cnidarians are diploblastic with tissue level organisation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The cnidarian digestive cavity is:
questions.explanation: Cnidarians have a gastrovascular cavity with a single mouth on the hypostome.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Digestion in cnidarians is:
questions.explanation: Cnidarians show both extracellular and intracellular digestion.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Coral skeleton is made of:
questions.explanation: Corals possess a calcium carbonate skeleton.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Medusa body form is:
questions.explanation: Medusa is umbrella-shaped and free-swimming (e.g., Aurelia); polyp is sessile and cylindrical.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Metagenesis is seen in:
questions.explanation: Obelia shows metagenesis: polyps produce medusae asexually; medusae produce polyps sexually.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Physalia is commonly known as:
questions.explanation: Physalia is the Portuguese man-of-war.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Gorgonia is called:
questions.explanation: Gorgonia is the sea fan.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Aurelia represents which cnidarian body form?
questions.explanation: Aurelia (jellyfish) is the medusa form.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ctenophores are commonly called:
questions.explanation: Ctenophores are sea walnuts or comb jellies, exclusively marine.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Locomotion in ctenophores is aided by:
questions.option_b: Eight rows of ciliated comb plates
questions.explanation: Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates help ctenophore locomotion.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Bioluminescence is a marked feature of:
questions.explanation: Ctenophores show well-marked bioluminescence.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ctenophore reproduction is:
questions.option_b: Sexual with external fertilisation and indirect development
questions.explanation: Ctenophores reproduce only sexually; fertilisation is external with indirect development.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which is an example of Ctenophora?
questions.explanation: Pleurobrachia and Ctenoplana are ctenophore examples.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ctenophores are:
questions.explanation: Ctenophores are marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic, tissue-level organisms.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Platyhelminthes are called flatworms because:
questions.option_a: They live on flat surfaces only
questions.explanation: Dorsoventral flattening gives platyhelminthes the name flatworms.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Platyhelminthes are:
questions.explanation: Flatworms are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, acoelomate with organ level organisation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Parasitic flatworms often possess:
questions.explanation: Parasitic platyhelminthes bear hooks and suckers for attachment.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Flame cells in flatworms function in:
questions.explanation: Flame cells aid osmoregulation and excretion in platyhelminthes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: High regeneration capacity is seen in:
questions.explanation: Planaria shows high regeneration capacity among platyhelminthes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Taenia is commonly known as:
questions.explanation: Taenia is the tapeworm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Fasciola is the:
questions.explanation: Fasciola is the liver fluke.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Platyhelminthes are mostly:
questions.explanation: Most platyhelminthes are endoparasites in animals including humans.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Aschelminthes are called roundworms because:
questions.option_a: They are coiled like a tape
questions.option_c: They live in round burrows only
questions.explanation: Circular cross-section gives aschelminths the name roundworms.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Aschelminthes are:
questions.explanation: Roundworms are bilateral, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate with organ-system organisation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Aschelminthes digestive tract is:
questions.explanation: Aschelminths have a complete alimentary canal with a muscular pharynx.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Aschelminthes are typically:
questions.option_b: Dioecious with females often longer than males
questions.explanation: Roundworms are dioecious; females are often longer than males.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Wuchereria causes:
questions.explanation: Wuchereria is the filaria worm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ancylostoma is the:
questions.explanation: Ancylostoma is the hookworm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Aschelminthes development can be:
questions.explanation: After internal fertilisation, aschelminths may show direct or indirect development.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Annelids are:
questions.explanation: Annelids are triploblastic, metamerically segmented coelomates.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The name Annelida refers to:
questions.explanation: Annelida comes from annulus (little ring), referring to body segmentation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Parapodia in Nereis help in:
questions.option_c: Gas exchange only in land forms
questions.explanation: Parapodia are lateral appendages aiding swimming in aquatic annelids like Nereis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Annelids possess:
questions.explanation: Annelids have a closed circulatory system.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Nephridia in annelids function in:
questions.explanation: Nephridia perform osmoregulation and excretion in annelids.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which annelid is dioecious?
questions.explanation: Nereis is dioecious; earthworms (Pheretima) and leeches are monoecious.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pheretima is the scientific name for:
questions.explanation: Pheretima is the earthworm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Hirudinaria is a:
questions.explanation: Hirudinaria is the blood-sucking leech.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The largest animal phylum is:
questions.explanation: Arthropoda is the largest phylum; over two-thirds of named species are arthropods.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Arthropod exoskeleton is made of:
questions.explanation: Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Jointed appendages characterise:
questions.explanation: Arthropoda means jointed appendages (arthros + poda).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Tracheal system as respiratory organ is found in:
questions.explanation: Arthropods may respire via gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae (insects).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Arthropods typically have:
questions.option_d: Single ventricle only in all cases
questions.explanation: Arthropods possess an open circulatory system.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Malpighian tubules are excretory structures in:
questions.explanation: Many arthropods excrete via Malpighian tubules.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Bombyx is the:
questions.explanation: Bombyx is the silkworm.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Anopheles is a:
questions.explanation: Anopheles is a mosquito vector among arthropod examples.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Locusta is a:
questions.explanation: Locusta is the gregarious locust pest.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Limulus is called:
questions.explanation: Limulus (king crab) is cited as a living fossil arthropod.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Typical arthropod body regions include:
questions.option_c: Mantle, foot and visceral hump only
questions.explanation: Arthropod body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The second largest animal phylum is:
questions.explanation: Mollusca is the second largest animal phylum after Arthropoda.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Typical molluscan body plan includes:
questions.option_a: Head, thorax, abdomen and chitinous exoskeleton
questions.option_b: Head, muscular foot and visceral hump with often a shell
questions.option_d: Disk, arms and water vascular system
questions.explanation: Molluscs have unsegmented body with head, muscular foot, visceral hump, often with calcareous shell.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Mantle cavity in molluscs contains:
questions.explanation: Mantle cavity houses feather-like gills with respiratory and excretory roles.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Radula is a feeding organ in:
questions.explanation: Molluscs possess a file-like rasping radula in the mouth.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pinctada is the:
questions.explanation: Pinctada is the pearl oyster.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Octopus is commonly called:
questions.explanation: Octopus is the devil fish.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sepia is the:
questions.explanation: Sepia is cuttlefish; Loligo is squid.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Molluscs are generally:
questions.explanation: Molluscs are usually dioecious, oviparous with indirect development.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Echinodermata means:
questions.explanation: Echinodermata refers to spiny skin from calcareous ossicles in the endoskeleton.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Echinoderm symmetry is:
questions.option_a: Bilateral in both larva and adult
questions.option_b: Radial in adult, bilateral in larva
questions.explanation: Adult echinoderms are radial; larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Water vascular system is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Water vascular system is the hallmark of echinoderms, aiding locomotion, feeding and respiration.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Echinoderms lack:
questions.explanation: Echinoderms have no distinct excretory system.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In echinoderms, mouth and anus are located:
questions.explanation: Echinoderms have complete gut with ventral mouth and dorsal anus.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Asterias is the:
questions.explanation: Asterias is the starfish.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Cucumaria is the:
questions.explanation: Cucumaria is the sea cucumber.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Echinoderms are:
questions.explanation: All echinoderms are marine.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Hemichordata is now classified as:
questions.explanation: Hemichordata is now a separate phylum under non-chordata, not a chordate subphylum.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Stomochord in hemichordates is:
questions.option_b: Rudimentary structure in collar region similar to notochord
questions.explanation: Stomochord (stomachord) in the collar region is rudimentary and notochord-like.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Hemichordate body regions are:
questions.explanation: Hemichordate body has proboscis, collar and trunk.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Excretion in hemichordates occurs through:
questions.explanation: Proboscis gland is the excretory organ in hemichordates.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Balanoglossus belongs to phylum:
questions.explanation: Balanoglossus and Saccoglossus are hemichordate examples.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Hemichordates have:
questions.explanation: Hemichordates show open circulation and respire through gills.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Fundamental chordate characters include:
questions.option_a: Ventral solid nerve cord and dorsal heart
questions.option_b: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits
questions.explanation: Chordates have notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and paired pharyngeal gill slits.

questions.question: Which structures are characteristic of all angiosperms despite their morphological diversity?
questions.option_a: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits
questions.explanation: All angiosperms possess roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits regardless of external morphological variation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In a flowering plant, the shoot system refers to:
questions.explanation: The root system is underground; the shoot system comprises all aerial parts above the ground.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In most dicotyledonous plants, the primary root develops from:
questions.explanation: In dicots, the radicle elongates directly to form the primary root that grows into the soil.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Mustard plant exhibits which type of root system?
questions.explanation: Mustard has a tap root system formed by the primary root and its branches.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Wheat plant has which type of root system?
questions.explanation: In monocots like wheat, short-lived primary root is replaced by many roots from the stem base forming a fibrous root system.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Adventitious roots arise from:
questions.option_b: Parts of the plant other than the radicle
questions.explanation: Adventitious roots develop from plant parts other than the radicle, as in grass, Monstera and banyan.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which is NOT a main function of the root system?
questions.explanation: Roots absorb water/minerals, anchor the plant, store food and synthesise PGRs; photosynthesis is primarily a leaf function.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The thimble-like structure covering the root apex is called:
questions.explanation: The root cap is a thimble-like protective structure at the root apex.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Cells in the region of meristematic activity of the root are characterised by:
questions.option_b: Small size, thin walls and dense protoplasm with repeated division
questions.explanation: Meristematic root cells are small, thin-walled, densely protoplasmic and divide repeatedly.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Growth of the root in length occurs mainly in the:
questions.explanation: Cells in the region of elongation undergo rapid enlargement, increasing root length.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The region proximal to the zone of elongation where cells differentiate and mature is called:
questions.explanation: The region of maturation lies proximal to elongation where cells differentiate and mature.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Root hairs are formed from epidermal cells in the region of maturation and function in:
questions.explanation: Thread-like root hairs from epidermal cells absorb water and minerals from soil.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The stem develops from:
questions.explanation: The stem originates from the plumule of the embryo during seed germination.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The axillary bud, which may develop into a branch, is found:
questions.option_b: In the axil of the leaf at a node
questions.explanation: Leaves develop at nodes and bear axillary buds that can grow into branches.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Leaves originate from shoot apical meristems and are arranged in:
questions.explanation: Leaves arise from shoot apical meristems and show acropetal (youngest at apex) arrangement.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis are:
questions.explanation: Leaves are the primary vegetative organs for photosynthesis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The three main parts of a typical leaf are:
questions.explanation: A typical leaf has leaf base, petiole (stalk) and lamina (blade).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Stipules are:
questions.option_b: Two lateral small leaf-like structures at the leaf base
questions.explanation: Stipules are small leaf-like lateral structures sometimes present at the leaf base.

questions.question: In monocotyledons, the leaf base often:
questions.option_b: Expands into a sheath covering the stem
questions.explanation: Monocot leaf bases expand into sheaths that partially or wholly cover the stem.

questions.question: The swollen leaf base in some leguminous plants is called:
questions.explanation: Pulvinus is the swollen leaf base found in some leguminous plants.

questions.question: Flexible petioles help leaves by:
questions.option_b: Allowing blade flutter to cool the leaf and bring fresh air
questions.explanation: Flexible petioles position the blade and allow fluttering that cools the leaf and refreshes air at the surface.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The prominent middle vein of the leaf blade is called:
questions.explanation: The lamina bears veins; the central prominent vein is the midrib.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Venation refers to:
questions.option_b: Arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina
questions.option_c: Arrangement of flowers on floral axis
questions.explanation: Venation is the pattern of veins and veinlets in the leaf lamina.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: When veinlets form a network in the lamina, the venation is:
questions.explanation: Reticulate venation shows a net-like pattern of veinlets.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Parallel venation is characterised by veins that:
questions.option_b: Run parallel to each other within the lamina
questions.option_c: Radiate from midrib only in dicots
questions.explanation: In parallel venation, veins run side by side without forming a net.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Reticulate venation is generally found in:
questions.explanation: Dicots generally have reticulate venation; parallel venation is typical of most monocots.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A compound leaf is formed when:
questions.option_a: Lamina incisions reach up to the midrib forming leaflets
questions.explanation: Compound leaves have lamina incisions extending to the midrib, dividing it into leaflets.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In a compound leaf, axillary bud is present:
questions.option_a: In the axil of each leaflet
questions.option_b: In the axil of petiole but not in axil of leaflets
questions.explanation: Axillary buds occur in petiole axils of both simple and compound leaves, never in leaflet axils.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Neem has which type of compound leaf?
questions.explanation: Neem has pinnately compound leaves with leaflets on a common axis (rachis) representing the midrib.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Silk cotton has:
questions.explanation: Silk cotton has palmately compound leaves with leaflets attached at the petiole tip.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Phyllotaxy refers to:
questions.option_b: Pattern of leaf arrangement on stem or branch
questions.explanation: Phyllotaxy describes how leaves are arranged on the stem or branch.

questions.question: Alternate phyllotaxy is seen in:
questions.explanation: Alternate phyllotaxy has one leaf per node in alternate positions; e.g., china rose, mustard, sunflower.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Opposite phyllotaxy is found in:
questions.explanation: Opposite phyllotaxy has paired leaves at each node lying opposite; e.g., Calotropis and guava.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Whorled phyllotaxy is exemplified by:
questions.explanation: Whorled phyllotaxy has more than two leaves forming a circle at a node, as in Alstonia.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A flower develops when:
questions.option_b: Shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem
questions.explanation: Flowers are modified shoots formed when shoot apical meristem becomes floral meristem.

questions.question: Inflorescence is:
questions.option_b: Arrangement of flowers on the floral axis
questions.explanation: Inflorescence refers to how flowers are arranged on the floral axis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In racemose inflorescence:
questions.option_a: Main axis terminates in a flower
questions.option_b: Main axis continues to grow; flowers borne laterally in acropetal order

questions.explanation: Racemose inflorescences have a continuously growing main axis with acropetal lateral flowers.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In cymose inflorescence:
questions.option_b: Main axis terminates in a flower; flowers in basipetal order
questions.explanation: Cymose inflorescences have limited growth with terminal flower and basipetal flower arrangement.

questions.question: When calyx and corolla are not distinct, they together form:
questions.explanation: In flowers like lily, undifferentiated calyx and corolla are called perianth.

questions.question: Mustard flower shows which symmetry?
questions.explanation: Actinomorphic flowers like mustard can be divided into equal halves in any radial plane.

questions.question: Pea flower is:
questions.explanation: Pea has zygomorphic (bilateral) symmetry— divisible into similar halves in one vertical plane only.

questions.question: An asymmetric flower example is:
questions.explanation: Canna has asymmetric (irregular) flowers not divisible into similar halves by any vertical plane.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A bracteate flower is one that:
questions.option_b: Has a reduced leaf (bract) at the base of the pedicel
questions.explanation: Bracteate flowers bear bracts (reduced leaves) at the pedicel base; without bracts they are ebracteate.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Mustard has which type of flower and ovary position?
questions.explanation: Mustard has hypogynous flowers with superior ovary (gynoecium at highest position).

questions.question: Half inferior ovary is seen in flowers of:
questions.explanation: Perigynous flowers like plum, rose and peach have half inferior ovary.

questions.explanation: Guava has epigynous flowers with inferior ovary enclosed by thalamus.

questions.question: Gamopetalous corolla has:
questions.explanation: Gamopetalous corolla has fused petals; polypetalous has free petals.

questions.question: Valvate aestivation is seen in:
questions.explanation: Valvate aestivation: members just touch at margins without overlapping, as in Calotropis.

questions.question: Imbricate aestivation occurs in:
questions.explanation: Imbricate aestivation has overlapping margins without fixed direction, as in Cassia and gulmohur.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Pea and bean show vexillary aestivation with standard, wings and keel petals.

questions.question: Pollen grains are produced in:
questions.explanation: Each bilobed anther has pollen-sacs in its lobes where pollen grains form.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Epipetalous stamens are found in:
questions.explanation: Epipetalous stamens are adnate to petals, as in brinjal; lily shows epiphyllous on perianth.

questions.question: When all stamens remain free, the androecium is:
questions.explanation: Polyandrous androecium has free (united) stamens.

questions.question: Diadelphous stamens are found in:
questions.explanation: Pea has diadelphous stamens united into two bundles; china rose is monoadelphous, citrus polyadelphous.

questions.question: Variation in filament length within a flower is seen in:
questions.explanation: Salvia and mustard show differing stamen filament lengths within the same flower.

questions.question: Apocarpous gynoecium is seen in:
questions.explanation: Apocarpous gynoecium has free carpels, as in lotus and rose.

questions.question: Syncarpous gynoecium is found in:
questions.explanation: Syncarpous gynoecium has fused carpels, as in mustard and tomato.

questions.question: Marginal placentation is seen in:

questions.question: Axile placentation occurs in:

questions.question: Basal placentation with a single ovule is seen in:
questions.explanation: Basal placentation has one ovule at the ovary base, as in sunflower and marigold.

questions.question: Radicle and plumule are located at:

questions.question: Each microsporangium contains:

questions.question: Fusion of petals in a flower is called:

questions.question: What is the study of the internal structure of plants called?
questions.explanation: Anatomy is the study of the internal structure and functional organisation of higher plants.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: What is the correct hierarchical organisation in plants?
questions.explanation: In plants, cells form tissues, and tissues are organised into organs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Within angiosperms, monocots and dicots differ primarily in their:
questions.explanation: Monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants show marked anatomical differences in their internal structures.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Internal structures of plants show:
questions.explanation: Plant internal structures exhibit adaptations suited to different environmental conditions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: How many types of tissue systems are recognised in flowering plants on the basis of structure and location?
questions.explanation: The three tissue systems are epidermal, ground (fundamental), and vascular (conducting).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three tissue systems in flowering plants?
questions.explanation: Meristematic tissue is a tissue type, not a tissue system. The three systems are epidermal, ground, and vascular.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The epidermal tissue system comprises:
questions.option_b: Epidermal cells, stomata, trichomes and hairs
questions.explanation: The epidermal tissue system includes epidermal cells, stomata, and epidermal appendages such as trichomes and hairs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The epidermis is:
questions.option_a: The innermost layer of the primary plant body
questions.option_b: The outermost layer of the primary plant body
questions.explanation: Epidermis forms the outermost covering layer of the primary plant body.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The epidermis is usually:
questions.explanation: Epidermis typically consists of a single layer of compactly arranged cells.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Epidermal cells are characteristically:
questions.option_b: Parenchymatous with small cytoplasm and a large vacuole
questions.explanation: Epidermal cells are parenchymatous, with cytoplasm lining the cell wall and a prominent vacuole.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The cuticle on the epidermis functions to:
questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle layer on the outside of the epidermis reduces water loss.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In which plant organ is the cuticle absent?
questions.explanation: Unlike aerial parts, roots lack a cuticle on their epidermis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Stomata in leaf epidermis regulate:
questions.explanation: Stomata control transpiration and the exchange of gases such as CO₂ and O₂.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Each stoma is composed of:
questions.option_b: Two bean-shaped guard cells enclosing a stomatal pore
questions.explanation: A stoma consists of two bean-shaped guard cells that surround the stomatal pore.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In grasses, guard cells are:
questions.explanation: Grass stomata have characteristic dumb-bell shaped guard cells.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In guard cells, wall thickness is characterised by:
questions.option_a: Thick outer walls and thin inner walls
questions.option_b: Thin outer walls and highly thickened inner walls
questions.explanation: Guard cells have thin outer walls and thickened inner walls toward the stomatal pore, enabling pore opening and closing.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Guard cells possess chloroplasts and:
questions.option_b: Regulate opening and closing of stomata
questions.explanation: Guard cells contain chloroplasts and control stomatal opening and closing through turgor changes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Specialised epidermal cells near guard cells are called:
questions.explanation: Subsidiary cells are specialised epidermal cells located in the vicinity of guard cells.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Stomatal apparatus includes:
questions.option_b: Stomatal aperture, guard cells and subsidiary cells
questions.explanation: The stomatal apparatus comprises the stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Root hairs are:
questions.option_b: Unicellular elongations of epidermal cells that absorb water and minerals
questions.explanation: Root hairs are unicellular extensions of epidermal cells specialised for absorption of water and minerals.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Epidermal hairs on the stem are called:
questions.explanation: Stem epidermal hairs are termed trichomes, distinct from unicellular root hairs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Trichomes in the shoot system are usually:
questions.explanation: Unlike root hairs, shoot trichomes are typically multicellular structures.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Trichomes help in:
questions.option_b: Preventing water loss due to transpiration
questions.explanation: Trichomes may be branched, soft or stiff, sometimes secretory, and help reduce transpirational water loss.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ground tissue includes all tissues except:
questions.explanation: Ground or fundamental tissue comprises all tissues other than the epidermis and vascular bundles.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ground tissue consists of simple tissues such as:
questions.explanation: Ground tissue is made up of the simple permanent tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Parenchymatous cells are usually present in:
questions.option_b: Cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays
questions.explanation: In primary stems and roots, parenchyma occurs in cortex, pericycle, pith, and medullary rays.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The ground tissue in leaves, consisting of thin-walled chloroplast-containing cells, is called:
questions.explanation: Leaf ground tissue with chloroplasts is termed mesophyll.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The vascular tissue system consists of which complex tissues?
questions.explanation: The vascular system is formed by the complex tissues xylem and phloem.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Vascular bundles are constituted by:
questions.explanation: A vascular bundle is formed by xylem and phloem together.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Open vascular bundles are so called because they:
questions.option_a: Lack cambium between xylem and phloem
questions.option_b: Have cambium between phloem and xylem and can form secondary tissues
questions.option_c: Have radial arrangement of xylem and phloem
questions.explanation: In dicot stems, cambium between xylem and phloem allows formation of secondary xylem and phloem, making bundles open.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Closed vascular bundles are characteristic of:
questions.option_b: Monocotyledons lacking cambium in vascular bundles

questions.question: Activation energy in an enzyme-catalysed reaction is:
questions.option_a: Energy difference between product and substrate
questions.option_b: Energy difference between substrate average and transition state
questions.option_c: Total heat released in exothermic reaction
questions.option_d: Energy of ES complex at equilibrium only
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the barrier between S and the transition state.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Catalytic proteins accelerate biochemical reactions chiefly by:
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy without changing overall ΔG.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In the mechanism E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P, formation of ES is:
questions.explanation: NCERT states ES complex formation is essential for catalysis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: When temperature is raised far above the optimum for a mesophilic enzyme:
questions.option_b: Protein denatures and activity is lost
questions.option_c: Only Km changes but Vmax is unchanged
questions.explanation: High temperature destroys tertiary structure—denaturation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: At very high substrate concentration, reaction velocity plateaus because:
questions.option_a: All enzyme active sites are occupied
questions.explanation: Beyond saturation, no free enzyme remains to bind additional substrate.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Malonate inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase is:
questions.explanation: Malonate structurally resembles succinate and competes for the active site.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In competitive inhibition, increasing substrate concentration will:
questions.option_a: Have no effect on reaction rate
questions.option_c: Reduce inhibitor binding and restore velocity toward Vmax
questions.explanation: Higher [S] outcompetes inhibitor for active site—classic NEET trap vs non-competitive.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A competitive inhibitor affects enzyme kinetics such that:
questions.option_a: Km appears increased but Vmax is unchanged
questions.option_b: Vmax is halved but Km unchanged
questions.option_c: Both Km and Vmax decrease equally
questions.option_d: Only activation energy increases without binding
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors raise apparent Km without changing Vmax—standard NEET kinetics trap.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A general rule of thumb for many chemical processes is that rate:
questions.option_b: Doubles or halves for every 10°C change
questions.explanation: NCERT states rate doubles or decreases by half per 10°C change.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Enzymes from thermophilic organisms differ from typical mesophilic enzymes by:
questions.explanation: Thermophile enzymes remain stable at high temperatures.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Catalytic nucleic acids are called:
questions.explanation: Some nucleic acids behave like enzymes—ribozymes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Enzymes that catalyse interconversion of optical or geometric isomers belong to:
questions.explanation: Isomerases catalyse isomer interconversions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Trypsin digesting proteins is an example of:
questions.explanation: Proteolytic enzymes hydrolyse peptide bonds—hydrolases.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: DNA ligase joining DNA fragments is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Ligases catalyse joining of two compounds.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: When a cofactor is removed from a conjugated enzyme, the remaining protein part is the:
questions.explanation: Apoenzyme lacks cofactor; holoenzyme is complete and active.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Haem in peroxidase is a:
questions.explanation: Prosthetic groups are organic and tightly bound to apoenzyme.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Coenzymes NAD and NADP contain the vitamin:
questions.explanation: Niacin is an essential component of NAD/NADP.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Carboxypeptidase requires which metal ion cofactor?
questions.explanation: Zinc forms coordination bonds at the active site of carboxypeptidase.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Lipids appear in the macromolecular fraction because they are large polymers.
Reason (R): Lipids have molecular weights exceeding 10,000 Da.
questions.option_a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.option_b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.option_c: A is true but R is false
questions.option_d: A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Lipids are <800 Da; they pellet due to membrane vesicles, not high MW.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Mesophilic enzymes lose activity at high temperature.
Reason (R): High temperature destroys tertiary structure by denaturation.
questions.option_a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.option_b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.option_c: A is true but R is false
questions.option_d: A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both true; denaturation explains loss of activity above optimum.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Reaction velocity reaches Vmax.
Reason (R): All enzyme molecules are already bound to substrate.
questions.option_a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.option_b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.option_c: A is true but R is false
questions.option_d: A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Saturation occurs when no free enzyme remains—R correctly explains A.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site.
Reason (R): Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.
questions.option_a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.option_b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.option_c: A is true but R is false
questions.option_d: A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both true but the specific example does not explain the general principle as R of A.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The acid-soluble pool contains micromolecules.
Reason (R): Their molecular weights range from about 18 to 800 Da.
questions.option_a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.option_b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.option_c: A is true but R is false
questions.option_d: A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Acid-soluble pool contains small biomolecules in that MW range.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:
Assertion (A): RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the biosphere.
Reason (R): It catalyses the first step of carbon fixation in all plants.
questions.option_a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.option_b: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.option_c: A is true but R is false
questions.option_d: A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both true; RuBisCO abundance reflects vast photosynthetic biomass but R is not the strict explanation of A.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:

questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Alpha-amino acids are defined by having:
questions.option_a: Amino and carboxyl groups on different carbons
questions.option_b: Amino and acidic groups as substituents on the same α-carbon

questions.explanation: Alpha-amino acids have both groups on the same α-carbon.

questions.question: Glutamic acid and lysine are examples of:
questions.option_a: Neutral and aromatic amino acids respectively
questions.explanation: Glutamic acid is acidic; lysine is basic.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Lecithin, containing phosphorus and a phosphorylated nitrogenous compound, is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Lecithin is a membrane phospholipid.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Oils remain liquid in winter because they:
questions.option_a: Have higher melting point than fats
questions.option_b: Have lower melting point than fats
questions.explanation: Oils have lower melting points; fats are solid at room temperature.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Arachidonic acid compared to palmitic acid has:
questions.option_b: More carbon atoms including carboxyl carbon
questions.explanation: Palmitic 16C; arachidonic 20C including carboxyl carbon.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Glucose to pyruvate via ten enzyme-catalysed steps is a:
questions.explanation: Multistep reactions catalysed by enzymes constitute a metabolic pathway.

questions.question: The same glycolytic pathway from glucose can yield:
questions.option_b: Pyruvate, lactic acid or ethanol depending on conditions
questions.explanation: Different cells produce different end products from pyruvate.

questions.question: The active site of an enzyme is best described as:
questions.option_b: A crevice or pocket where substrate binds
questions.explanation: Active site is a pocket in tertiary structure where substrate fits.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: An enzyme showing maximum activity at a particular pH and decline on either side is demonstrating:
questions.option_b: Effect of pH on tertiary structure and activity
questions.explanation: pH affects ionisation of active site residues—optimum pH curve.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Below optimum temperature, enzyme activity is lower mainly because:
questions.option_b: Molecular collisions and flexibility are reduced
questions.explanation: Low T reduces activity; high T denatures—NEET distinction.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A major difference between inorganic catalysts and enzymes is:
questions.option_b: Enzymes are damaged at high temperatures unlike many inorganic catalysts
questions.explanation: Enzymes denature at high T; inorganic catalysts often need high T/pressure.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Invertase hydrolyses sucrose into:
questions.explanation: Invertase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Glycerol is chemically:
questions.explanation: Glycerol is trihydroxy propane.

questions.question: Palmitic acid as a saturated fatty acid has:
questions.option_a: One or more C=C double bonds
questions.explanation: Saturated fatty acids lack double bonds.
