questions.explanation: Eosinophils combat parasites/allergy.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pulmonary artery carries:
questions.option_a: Deoxygenated blood from RV to lungs
questions.explanation: Only pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood to heart.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Only artery carrying oxygenated blood in adult humans is:
questions.option_a: Pulmonary artery is deoxygenated; pulmonary vein oxygenated
questions.option_d: All arteries O2-rich including pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: NEET trap: pulmonary artery = deoxygenated; pulmonary vein = oxygenated.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Assertion (A): Human blood volume is about 5 litres in adult. Reason (R): Plasma constitutes about 55% of blood volume. Choose the correct option:
questions.option_a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.option_b: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.option_c: A is true but R is false
questions.option_d: A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Plasma is major fraction of blood volume.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which chamber receives oxygenated blood from lungs?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins deliver O2-rich blood to left atrium.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Second heart sound (dub) is due to closure of:
questions.explanation: Dub: aortic and pulmonary valve closure.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: P wave on ECG indicates:
questions.explanation: P wave precedes atrial contraction.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A person with blood group O has:
questions.option_a: No A or B antigens on RBC; anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma
questions.option_d: Rh antigen always without any antibodies
questions.explanation: Group O lacks A/B antigens; has both antibodies.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: First pregnancy Rh- mother carrying Rh+ fetus usually:
questions.option_a: May be unaffected; sensitisation risk increases in subsequent Rh+ pregnancies
questions.option_c: Converts mother to AB positive blood group
questions.option_d: Eliminates all maternal antibodies permanently first exposure
questions.explanation: Sensitisation often after first exposure; second pregnancy higher risk.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Eosinophils increase in:
questions.explanation: Eosinophils combat parasites and modulate allergy.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which cascade is initiated during blood coagulation?
questions.option_a: Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by thrombin
questions.option_b: Direct conversion of RBC to WBC
questions.option_d: Plasma to serum without clotting factors
questions.explanation: Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen forming fibrin mesh.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Cardiac impulse originates at:
questions.option_d: Bundle of His only in atria
questions.explanation: SA node sets intrinsic heart rate.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood?
questions.option_d: Right ventricle outflow to lungs before oxygenation
questions.explanation: Pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood from lungs to heart.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Compared to blood plasma, lymph has:
questions.option_d: Identical cell count to arterial blood
questions.explanation: Lymph is interstitial fluid with fewer proteins.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Human heart is:
questions.option_a: Myogenic with SA node initiating beat
questions.option_b: Neurogenic requiring CNS for every beat
questions.explanation: Myogenic: cardiac muscle initiates rhythm intrinsically.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: If heart rate is 72/min and stroke volume 70 mL, cardiac output is approximately:
questions.explanation: CO = 72 × 70 = 5040 mL/min ≈ 5 L/min.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Advantage of double circulation in mammals includes:
questions.option_a: Maintaining high systemic blood pressure for efficient tissue perfusion
questions.option_c: Mixing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in ventricle
questions.option_d: Single circuit serving gills and body together
questions.explanation: Separate circuits maintain high pressure to systemic tissues.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ca2+ is essential for several clotting steps
2. Haemophilia involves deficiency of clotting factor VIII or IX
3. Platelets are unnecessary for coagulation
Which of the following combinations is correct?
questions.explanation: Platelets essential; statements 1 and 2 correct.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Histamine release during allergy primarily from:
questions.explanation: Basophils/mast cells release histamine in allergy.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: AV node delay allows:
questions.option_a: Atria to complete contraction before ventricular systole
questions.option_c: Simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction always
questions.explanation: Brief AV delay synchronises atrial then ventricular beat.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Closed circulatory system is found in:
questions.option_b: Cockroach only among listed complex animals
questions.explanation: Annelids and vertebrates have closed circulation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Adrenaline during stress causes:
questions.option_a: Increased heart rate and force of contraction
questions.option_b: Bradycardia and vasodilation everywhere without exception
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation increases HR and contractility.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Angiotensin II primarily causes:
questions.option_d: Elimination of all Na+ in urine without retention
questions.explanation: Angiotensin II is potent vasoconstrictor.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: B-lymphocytes are primarily responsible for:
questions.option_b: Direct phagocytosis of all bacteria without antibodies
questions.explanation: B cells differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which of the following substances may accumulate in animals and need to be eliminated?
questions.option_a: Ammonia, urea, uric acid, CO₂, water and ions only
questions.option_d: Ammonia, urea, uric acid, CO₂, water, Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, phosphate and sulphate
questions.explanation: Animals accumulate various metabolic and ingested wastes including nitrogenous compounds, gases, water and ions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Among ammonia, urea and uric acid, which statement is correct regarding toxicity and water requirement?
questions.option_a: Uric acid is most toxic and needs most water
questions.option_b: Ammonia is most toxic and needs large amounts of water; uric acid is least toxic with minimum water loss
questions.option_c: Urea is most toxic and ammonia needs least water
questions.option_d: All three have equal toxicity and water requirements
questions.explanation: Ammonia is most toxic and water-demanding; uric acid is least toxic and conserves water.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The process of excreting ammonia as the primary nitrogenous waste is called:
questions.explanation: Excretion of ammonia is termed ammonotelism.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which group of animals is primarily ammonotelic?
questions.option_c: Many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects
questions.option_d: Marine fishes and desert reptiles only
questions.explanation: Aquatic animals with abundant water commonly excrete ammonia directly.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: How is ammonia typically eliminated in fishes?
questions.option_a: By active secretion into renal tubules only
questions.option_b: By conversion to uric acid in the liver
questions.option_c: By diffusion across body or gill surfaces as ammonium ions
questions.option_d: By storage in the urinary bladder as crystals
questions.explanation: Soluble ammonia diffuses out through body or gill surfaces as ammonium ions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In ammonotelic animals, the kidneys:
questions.option_a: Are the primary organs for ammonia removal
questions.option_b: Do not play any significant role in ammonia removal
questions.option_c: Convert ammonia to urea before excretion
questions.option_d: Store ammonia until it forms uric acid
questions.explanation: In ammonotelic animals, ammonia is removed mainly by diffusion, not kidneys.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Why did terrestrial adaptation favour urea and uric acid over ammonia as nitrogenous wastes?
questions.option_a: They are more toxic and easier to filter
questions.option_b: They are less toxic and help conserve water
questions.option_c: They require more water for elimination
questions.option_d: They can only be excreted through gills
questions.explanation: Less toxic urea and uric acid allow water conservation on land.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ureotelic animals include:
questions.option_c: Mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes
questions.explanation: Mammals, terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes mainly excrete urea.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In ureotelic animals, urea is formed in the _____ and excreted by the _____.
questions.explanation: The liver converts ammonia to urea; kidneys filter and excrete it.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In some ureotelic animals, urea retained in the kidney matrix helps to:
questions.explanation: Retained urea in kidney matrix aids osmolarity regulation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Uricotelic animals excrete nitrogenous waste as:
questions.option_b: Urea in large volumes of dilute urine
questions.option_c: Uric acid as pellet or paste with minimum water loss
questions.option_d: Amino acids through Malpighian tubules only
questions.explanation: Uricotelic animals excrete uric acid with minimal water loss.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Flame cells or protonephridia are excretory structures found in:
questions.option_c: Flatworms, rotifers, some annelids and Amphioxus
questions.explanation: Protonephridia occur in flatworms, rotifers, some annelids and Amphioxus.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The primary function of protonephridia is:
questions.explanation: Protonephridia mainly regulate ionic and fluid balance.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Nephridia are the excretory structures of:
questions.explanation: Nephridia are tubular excretory organs of annelids.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Nephridia in annelids function to:
questions.option_b: Remove nitrogenous wastes and maintain fluid and ionic balance
questions.explanation: Nephridia eliminate nitrogenous wastes and help osmoregulation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Malpighian tubules serve as excretory structures in:
questions.explanation: Most insects, including cockroaches, have Malpighian tubules.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Malpighian tubules in insects help in:
questions.option_b: Removal of nitrogenous wastes and osmoregulation
questions.explanation: Malpighian tubules excrete nitrogenous wastes and aid osmoregulation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Antennal or green glands are excretory organs of:
questions.explanation: Green/antennal glands excrete wastes in crustaceans.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Vertebrate excretory organs are:
questions.explanation: Vertebrates possess complex tubular kidneys.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The human excretory system consists of:
questions.option_a: One kidney, one ureter, bladder and urethra
questions.option_b: A pair of kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra
questions.option_d: Kidneys connected directly to urethra without ureters
questions.explanation: Humans have paired kidneys and ureters, plus bladder and urethra.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Human kidneys are located:
questions.option_a: In the pelvic cavity below the bladder
questions.option_b: Between last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra, near dorsal abdominal wall
questions.option_c: In the thoracic cavity adjacent to the heart
questions.option_d: In the scrotum outside the abdominal cavity
questions.explanation: Kidneys lie retroperitoneally between T12 and L3 vertebrae.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The approximate dimensions and weight of an adult human kidney are:
questions.option_a: 5 cm length, 2 cm width, 50 g weight
questions.option_b: 10-12 cm length, 5-7 cm width, 2-3 cm thickness, 120-170 g weight
questions.option_c: 20 cm length, 10 cm width, 500 g weight
questions.option_d: 8 cm length, 8 cm width, 300 g weight
questions.explanation: Adult kidneys measure about 10-12 × 5-7 × 2-3 cm and weigh 120-170 g.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The hilum of the kidney is the site where enter:
questions.explanation: Hilum is the entry/exit point for ureter, vessels and nerves.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The broad funnel-shaped space inner to the hilum with calyceal projections is the:
questions.explanation: Renal pelvis is a funnel-shaped cavity with calyces.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The two main zones of the kidney are:
questions.explanation: Kidney has outer cortex and inner medulla.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Medullary pyramids are:
questions.option_a: Outer cortical extensions into the capsule
questions.option_b: Conical masses in the medulla projecting into calyces
questions.option_d: Branches of the renal artery only
questions.explanation: Medullary pyramids are conical medullary structures opening into calyces.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Columns of Bertini are:
questions.option_b: Cortical tissue extending between medullary pyramids
questions.option_c: Collecting ducts in the renal pelvis
questions.explanation: Columns of Bertini are cortical columns between pyramids.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The functional unit of the kidney is:
questions.option_b: The nephron (nearly one million per kidney)
questions.explanation: Each kidney contains about one million nephrons as functional units.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A nephron consists of:
questions.explanation: Each nephron has a glomerulus and a renal tubule.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The glomerulus is formed by:
questions.option_a: A tuft of capillaries from the afferent arteriole (branch of renal artery)
questions.option_b: Venous capillaries from the renal vein
questions.option_d: The efferent arteriole alone without capillaries
questions.explanation: Afferent arteriole forms the glomerular capillary tuft.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Bowman's capsule is:
questions.option_a: A single-walled tube in the medulla
questions.option_b: A double-walled cup-like structure enclosing the glomerulus
questions.option_c: The collecting duct opening into calyces
questions.option_d: The outer tough capsule of the kidney
questions.explanation: Bowman's capsule is a double-walled cup enclosing the glomerulus.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The Malpighian body or renal corpuscle consists of:
questions.explanation: Renal corpuscle = glomerulus + Bowman's capsule.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Henle's loop is characterised by:
questions.option_b: A hairpin shape with descending and ascending limbs
questions.explanation: Henle's loop is hairpin-shaped with descending and ascending limbs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Collecting ducts ultimately open into the renal pelvis through:
questions.explanation: Collecting ducts drain via medullary pyramids into calyces and renal pelvis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Cortical nephrons are characterised by:
questions.option_a: A very long loop of Henle extending deep into medulla
questions.option_b: A short loop of Henle extending only slightly into medulla
questions.explanation: Most nephrons are cortical with short Henle's loops.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Juxtamedullary nephrons have:
questions.option_b: A very long loop of Henle running deep into the medulla
questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops deep in the medulla.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Peritubular capillaries are formed by:
questions.option_a: The afferent arteriole before the glomerulus
questions.option_b: The efferent arteriole forming a network around the renal tubule
questions.option_c: Branches of the renal vein only
questions.explanation: Efferent arteriole gives rise to peritubular capillaries around tubules.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Vasa recta are:
questions.option_b: U-shaped capillaries parallel to Henle's loop; absent or reduced in cortical nephrons
questions.option_d: Veins draining directly into the ureter
questions.explanation: Vasa recta run parallel to Henle's loop and are reduced in cortical nephrons.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The three main processes of urine formation are:
questions.option_c: Osmosis, diffusion and active transport only in bladder
questions.explanation: Urine formation involves filtration, reabsorption and secretion.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The kidneys filter approximately _____ ml of blood per minute, about _____ of ventricular output.
questions.explanation: Kidneys filter 1100-1200 ml blood/min, roughly one-fifth of cardiac output.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Glomerular filtration occurs through three layers:
questions.option_b: Glomerular endothelium, basement membrane and Bowman's capsule epithelium
questions.option_c: PCT epithelium, DCT epithelium and collecting duct
questions.option_d: Afferent arteriole wall, efferent arteriole wall and ureter
questions.explanation: Filtration barrier has endothelium, basement membrane and podocyte epithelium.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Podocytes of Bowman's capsule form:
questions.option_b: Filtration slits or slit pores between intricate cell arrangements
questions.option_d: The muscular wall of the ureter
questions.explanation: Podocytes create filtration slits for ultrafiltration.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Glomerular filtration is called ultrafiltration because:
questions.option_a: Only water passes; no solutes filter
questions.option_b: All plasma constituents except proteins pass into Bowman's capsule
questions.option_c: Only proteins are filtered into the capsule
questions.option_d: Blood cells and proteins both pass freely
questions.explanation: Ultrafiltration allows all plasma solutes except proteins to pass.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy individual is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal GFR is about 125 ml/min, totalling ~180 L filtrate per day.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is formed at the contact between:
questions.option_d: Henle's loop and vasa recta only
questions.explanation: JGA lies where DCT contacts the afferent arteriole.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A fall in GFR causes JG cells to release renin, which:
questions.option_b: Stimulates glomerular blood flow and restores GFR toward normal
questions.option_d: Converts urea to uric acid in the liver
questions.explanation: Renin release helps restore glomerular blood flow and GFR.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed by renal tubules?
questions.explanation: About 99% of filtrate is reabsorbed; only ~1.5 L becomes urine.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: During tubular reabsorption, glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed mainly by:
questions.explanation: Glucose, amino acids and Na⁺ are actively reabsorbed.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Tubular secretion involves movement of which substances into the filtrate?
questions.explanation: Tubular cells secrete H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia into filtrate.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The brush border epithelium of PCT serves to:
questions.option_d: Form the filtration barrier with podocytes
questions.explanation: Brush border microvilli increase absorptive surface in PCT.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs:
questions.option_b: Nearly all essential nutrients and 70-80% of electrolytes and water
questions.explanation: PCT reabsorbs most nutrients and 70-80% of electrolytes and water.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: PCT helps maintain pH balance by:
questions.option_b: Secreting H⁺ and ammonia and absorbing HCO₃⁻
questions.explanation: PCT secretes H⁺ and NH₃ while reabsorbing HCO₃⁻ for pH balance.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The ascending limb of Henle's loop:
questions.option_b: Has minimum reabsorption but helps maintain high medullary osmolarity
questions.explanation: Ascending limb has little reabsorption but builds medullary osmolarity.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The descending limb of Henle's loop is:
questions.option_a: Impermeable to water, permeable to electrolytes
questions.option_b: Permeable to water, almost impermeable to electrolytes
questions.option_c: Impermeable to both water and electrolytes
questions.explanation: Descending limb allows water out but not electrolytes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The ascending limb of Henle's loop is:
questions.option_a: Permeable to water, impermeable to electrolytes
questions.option_b: Impermeable to water but allows electrolyte transport
questions.option_c: Permeable to both water and proteins
questions.option_d: The main site of glucose reabsorption
questions.explanation: Ascending limb is water-impermeable but transports electrolytes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Reabsorption of Na⁺ and water in the DCT is:
questions.explanation: DCT reabsorbs Na⁺ and water conditionally under hormonal control.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The collecting duct is important for urine concentration because:
questions.option_a: It filters blood like the glomerulus
questions.option_b: Large amounts of water can be reabsorbed here to concentrate urine
questions.option_c: It is the only site of glomerular filtration
questions.explanation: Collecting duct reabsorbs water under ADH to concentrate urine.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The collecting duct contributes to medullary osmolarity by:
questions.option_b: Allowing small amounts of urea into medullary interstitium
questions.explanation: Some urea diffuses into medullary interstitium from collecting duct.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Counter-current in Henle's loop refers to:
questions.option_a: Filtrate flowing in the same direction in both limbs
questions.option_b: Filtrate flowing in opposite directions in the two limbs
questions.option_c: Blood flowing only through vasa recta
questions.explanation: Opposite flow in descending and ascending limbs creates counter-current.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The osmolarity gradient in the kidney interstitium ranges from approximately:
questions.option_a: 1200 mOsmol/L in cortex to 300 mOsmol/L in medulla
questions.option_b: 300 mOsmol/L in cortex to 1200 mOsmol/L in inner medulla
questions.option_d: 50 mOsmol/L in cortex to 50 mOsmol/L in medulla
questions.explanation: Interstitial osmolarity rises from 300 (cortex) to 1200 mOsmol/L (inner medulla).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The medullary osmolarity gradient is mainly established by:
questions.explanation: NaCl and urea are chief solutes creating the medullary gradient.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The counter-current mechanism involves the coordinated function of:
questions.explanation: Counter-current mechanism depends on Henle's loop and vasa recta arrangement.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Human kidneys can concentrate urine to approximately:
questions.option_b: Four times the concentration of initial filtrate
questions.option_d: Half the concentration of plasma only
questions.explanation: Human urine can be about four times more concentrated than initial filtrate.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Kidney function is regulated by hormonal feedback involving:
questions.option_b: Hypothalamus, JGA and to some extent the heart
questions.explanation: Hypothalamus, JGA and heart (ANF) regulate kidney function.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Excessive fluid loss stimulates release of ADH (vasopressin) from:
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptor activation leads to ADH release from neurohypophysis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: ADH acts on the kidney by:
questions.option_b: Facilitating water reabsorption from latter tubule parts, reducing urine volume
questions.explanation: ADH promotes water reabsorption in distal nephron, antidiuresis.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: ADH can indirectly increase GFR by:
questions.option_b: Constricting blood vessels, raising blood pressure and glomerular blood flow
questions.explanation: ADH vasoconstriction raises BP, which can increase GFR.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Renin acts on _____ to ultimately form _____.
questions.option_b: Angiotensinogen; angiotensin I and then angiotensin II
questions.explanation: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, then to angiotensin II.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Angiotensin II increases GFR primarily by:
questions.option_b: Acting as a powerful vasoconstrictor, raising glomerular blood pressure
questions.explanation: Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor that raises glomerular pressure and GFR.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Aldosterone, stimulated by angiotensin II, causes:
questions.option_b: Reabsorption of Na⁺ and water from distal tubule parts
questions.option_d: Conversion of urea to ammonia in PCT
questions.explanation: Aldosterone promotes Na⁺ and water reabsorption in distal nephron.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF) is released when:
questions.explanation: Increased atrial stretch from high blood flow triggers ANF release.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: ANF opposes the renin-angiotensin system by:
questions.option_a: Causing vasoconstriction and raising blood pressure
questions.option_b: Causing vasodilation and decreasing blood pressure
questions.explanation: ANF promotes vasodilation and lowers BP, countering renin-angiotensin.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Urine is stored in the urinary bladder until:
questions.option_b: A voluntary signal from the CNS initiates release
questions.explanation: Bladder stores urine until CNS-mediated voluntary voiding.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The micturition reflex is initiated by:
questions.option_b: Stretching of the urinary bladder as it fills
questions.explanation: Bladder distension triggers stretch receptors initiating micturition.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: During micturition, the CNS causes:
questions.option_b: Bladder smooth muscle contraction and urethral sphincter relaxation
questions.option_d: Only passive dripping without muscle action
questions.explanation: Voiding requires bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Micturition and micturition reflex respectively refer to:
questions.option_b: Release of urine; neural mechanism causing it
questions.option_c: Reabsorption of water; ADH action only
questions.explanation: Micturition is urine release; micturition reflex is its neural control.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Average daily urine output in a healthy adult human is:
questions.explanation: Daily urine volume averages 1-1.5 litres despite ~180 L filtrate.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Normal human urine is typically:
questions.option_b: Light yellow, slightly acidic (pH ~6.0), with characteristic odour
questions.explanation: Normal urine is light yellow, slightly acidic (~pH 6) with characteristic smell.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Average daily urea excretion in humans is approximately:
questions.explanation: Humans excrete roughly 25-30 g urea per day.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Glycosuria and ketonuria in urine may indicate:
questions.option_d: High protein diet without metabolic disorder
questions.explanation: Glucose and ketone bodies in urine suggest diabetes mellitus.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The lungs contribute to excretion by removing approximately:
questions.option_a: 200 mL CO₂ per minute and significant water daily
questions.explanation: Lungs excrete ~200 mL CO₂/min and considerable water vapour.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The liver aids excretion by secreting bile containing:
questions.option_b: Bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroids, vitamins and drugs
questions.explanation: Bile carries various waste products including bilirubin and drug metabolites.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Human sweat contains:
questions.option_b: NaCl, small amounts of urea, lactic acid, etc.
questions.option_c: Large amounts of uric acid pellets
questions.explanation: Sweat is a watery fluid with NaCl, urea and lactic acid among other solutes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The primary function of sweat is:
questions.option_a: Excretion of nitrogenous wastes as main role
questions.option_b: Cooling the body surface; also removes some wastes secondarily
questions.option_c: Production of sebum for skin protection
questions.explanation: Sweat mainly cools the body but also eliminates some wastes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Sebaceous glands excrete substances such as:
questions.option_b: Sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through sebum
questions.explanation: Sebum carries sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes to the skin surface.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Uremia is:
questions.option_b: Accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction
questions.explanation: Uremia is dangerous urea buildup in blood from failed kidney function.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: During haemodialysis, blood is drawn from an artery and:
questions.option_a: Filtered directly in the liver without anticoagulant
questions.option_b: Pumped to a dialysing unit after adding anticoagulant like heparin
questions.explanation: Arterial blood with heparin enters the artificial kidney unit.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Dialysing fluid in haemodialysis has composition:
questions.option_a: Identical to urine including all wastes
questions.option_b: Same as plasma except nitrogenous wastes are absent
questions.option_d: Higher urea than blood to draw wastes in
questions.explanation: Dialysate matches plasma minus nitrogenous wastes for diffusion out.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: After haemodialysis, cleared blood is returned to the body via a vein with:
questions.explanation: Anti-heparin is added before returning blood to reverse anticoagulation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Kidney transplantation for renal failure preferably uses a donor kidney from:
questions.option_a: Any unrelated donor without tissue matching
questions.option_b: A close relative to minimise immune rejection
questions.option_d: The patient's own failed kidney reimplanted
questions.explanation: Close relative donors reduce likelihood of immune rejection.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Renal calculi (kidney stones) are:
questions.option_b: Insoluble masses of crystallised salts like oxalates within the kidney

questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The neural system provides coordination through:

questions.question: Neurons are specialised cells that can:

questions.question: In insects, the neural system includes:

questions.explanation: Insects have a better organised neural system with a brain, ganglia and neural tissues.

questions.question: Compared to lower invertebrates, vertebrates possess:

questions.question: The human neural system is divided into:

questions.question: The peripheral neural system (PNS) comprises:

questions.question: Efferent nerve fibres transmit impulses:

questions.option_b: From the CNS to peripheral tissues/organs

questions.question: The somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to:

questions.question: The autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to:

questions.question: The autonomic neural system is subdivided into:

questions.question: The visceral nervous system is:

questions.question: A neuron is composed of three major parts:
questions.option_c: Schwann cell, myelin and node of Ranvier only
questions.option_d: Synaptic cleft, vesicles and receptors only
questions.explanation: The three main structural parts of a neuron are cell body, dendrites and axon.

questions.question: Granular bodies present in the neuronal cell body are called:
questions.explanation: Nissl's granules are characteristic granular bodies in the neuronal cell body.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Dendrites transmit nerve impulses:
questions.explanation: Dendrites carry impulses toward the neuronal cell body.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The axon of a neuron is characterised by:
questions.option_a: Short repeatedly branching fibres projecting from the cell body
questions.option_b: A long fibre with a branched distal end
questions.option_c: Absence of any branching at the terminal
questions.option_d: Presence of Nissl's granules along its entire length
questions.explanation: The axon is a long fibre that branches at its distal end.

questions.question: The bulb-like structure at the axon terminal containing neurotransmitters is called:
questions.explanation: Axon branches end in synaptic knobs that store neurotransmitters in vesicles.

questions.question: Axons transmit nerve impulses:

questions.question: Bipolar neurons are found in:

questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Unipolar neurons are typically found:
questions.option_a: In the cerebral cortex of adults
questions.option_b: In the retina of the eye

questions.question: Myelinated nerve fibres are enveloped by:

questions.option_b: Pia mater forming a myelin sheath
questions.option_d: Nodes of Ranvier without Schwann cells
questions.explanation: Schwann cells wrap around axons to form the myelin sheath in myelinated fibres.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths on an axon are called:
questions.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are the unmyelinated gaps between successive myelin segments.

questions.question: Myelinated nerve fibres are commonly found in:
questions.explanation: Spinal and cranial nerves contain myelinated nerve fibres.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Unmyelinated nerve fibres are commonly found in:
questions.explanation: Unmyelinated fibres, enclosed by Schwann cells without myelin, occur in autonomic and somatic systems.

questions.question: Neurons are excitable cells because their membranes are:
questions.explanation: Polarisation of the neural membrane makes neurons excitable.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ion channels on the neural membrane are:
questions.explanation: Neural membrane ion channels show selective permeability to specific ions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In a resting neuron, the axonal membrane is:
questions.option_a: More permeable to Na⁺ and impermeable to K⁺
questions.option_b: More permeable to K⁺ and nearly impermeable to Na⁺
questions.option_c: Equally permeable to Na⁺ and K⁺
questions.option_d: Impermeable to both Na⁺ and K⁺
questions.explanation: At rest, the axonal membrane favours K⁺ permeability over Na⁺.

questions.question: At rest, the axonal membrane is impermeable to:

questions.explanation: Negatively charged axoplasmic proteins cannot cross the resting membrane.

questions.question: The axoplasm inside a resting axon contains:

questions.question: Extracellular fluid surrounding a resting axon has:
questions.explanation: The outside fluid is low in K⁺ and high in Na⁺, creating an ionic gradient.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The sodium-potassium pump transports:
questions.option_c: Equal Na⁺ and K⁺ in both directions
questions.option_d: Only K⁺ out of the cell
questions.explanation: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump actively moves 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in.

questions.question: In a polarised resting axonal membrane:
questions.option_a: The outer surface is negative and inner surface positive
questions.option_b: The outer surface is positive and inner surface negative
questions.option_c: Both surfaces carry equal positive charges
questions.explanation: Resting polarisation gives the outer membrane surface a positive charge and the inner surface a negative charge.

questions.question: The electrical potential difference across the resting neural membrane is called:
questions.explanation: The resting potential is the voltage difference across a non-conducting neural membrane.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: When a stimulus is applied to a polarised axonal membrane, the stimulated site becomes:

questions.explanation: Stimulation increases Na⁺ permeability at the site of excitation.

questions.question: Rapid Na⁺ influx during excitation causes:
questions.option_b: Reversal of polarity with negative outer and positive inner surface
questions.option_c: Permanent loss of all membrane potential
questions.option_d: Increased K⁺ influx before Na⁺ entry
questions.explanation: Na⁺ influx reverses membrane polarity at the site of stimulation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Reversal of membrane polarity at the site of stimulation is termed:
questions.explanation: Polarity reversal at an excited site is called depolarisation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A nerve impulse is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The action potential at an excited site constitutes the nerve impulse.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: During impulse conduction along an axon, local current flows:
questions.option_a: On inner surface from depolarised to adjacent polarised region; on outer surface in opposite direction

questions.question: Nerve impulse conduction along an axon occurs by:
questions.option_a: A single depolarisation at the cell body only
questions.option_b: Repeated generation of action potentials along the axon length
questions.option_c: Diffusion of neurotransmitters through the axoplasm
questions.option_d: Passive flow of hormones in blood

questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Stimulus-induced increase in Na⁺ permeability of the axonal membrane is:
questions.explanation: Increased Na⁺ permeability during excitation lasts only briefly.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Restoration of resting potential after excitation involves:
questions.option_b: Increased K⁺ permeability and K⁺ efflux
questions.option_c: Permanent closure of all ion channels
questions.explanation: K⁺ efflux following increased K⁺ permeability repolarises the membrane to resting potential.

questions.question: Transmission of a nerve impulse from one neuron to another occurs through:
questions.explanation: Synapses are the junctions between neurons for impulse transmission.

questions.question: A synapse is formed by:

questions.question: The two types of synapses are:

questions.question: At electrical synapses, impulse transmission occurs by:

questions.option_d: Active transport of Na⁺ across synaptic cleft
questions.explanation: Electrical synapses allow direct current flow between adjacent neurons.

questions.question: Compared to chemical synapses, electrical synapses transmit impulses:

questions.question: Electrical synapses in the human neural system are:
questions.explanation: Electrical synapses occur infrequently in the human nervous system.

questions.question: At a chemical synapse, pre- and post-synaptic membranes are separated by:
questions.option_c: Direct membrane fusion without any gap
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses have a fluid-filled synaptic cleft between neuronal membranes.

questions.question: Chemicals involved in transmission at chemical synapses are called:
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters mediate chemical synaptic transmission.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Arrival of an action potential at the axon terminal causes:
questions.option_a: Immediate closure of all ion channels permanently
questions.option_b: Synaptic vesicles to move, fuse with membrane and release neurotransmitters
questions.option_c: Direct electrical current flow without vesicle movement
questions.explanation: Action potentials trigger vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the cleft.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Released neurotransmitters in a chemical synapse bind to:
questions.option_a: Receptors on the pre-synaptic membrane only
questions.option_b: Specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters act on specific receptors located on the post-synaptic membrane.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Binding of neurotransmitters to post-synaptic receptors can generate:
questions.explanation: Post-synaptic receptor activation may produce excitatory or inhibitory potentials.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The brain functions as:
questions.option_a: Only a storage organ for neurotransmitters
questions.option_b: The central information processing organ and command and control system

questions.question: Hydra nervous organisation is:

questions.question: Post-synaptic potentials may be:

questions.question: Which mode of reproduction is exhibited by all flowering plants?
questions.explanation: Every flowering plant (angiosperm) reproduces sexually through flowers.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In angiosperms, sexual reproduction takes place in:
questions.explanation: Flowers are the specialised organs where sexual reproduction occurs in flowering plants.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The male and female reproductive organs of a flower are respectively:
questions.explanation: Androecium (stamens) is male; gynoecium (pistil) is female.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Male and female gametophytes develop respectively in:
questions.option_b: Anther and embryo sac within ovule
questions.explanation: Pollen grains (male gametophytes) form in anthers; embryo sac (female gametophyte) forms in ovules.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Formation of a flower on a plant is preceded by:
questions.option_b: Hormonal and structural changes leading to floral primordium differentiation
questions.explanation: Flowering involves hormonal and structural changes that initiate floral primordium development.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The two parts of a typical stamen are:
questions.explanation: A stamen consists of a filament (stalk) and an anther (pollen-bearing part).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A typical angiosperm anther is:
questions.explanation: Each anther lobe contains two theca, making the anther bilobed and dithecous.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: How many microsporangia are present in a typical angiosperm anther?
questions.explanation: The tetragonal anther has four microsporangia, two in each lobe.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Mature microsporangia are also called:
questions.explanation: Developing microsporangia differentiate into pollen sacs filled with pollen grains.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The four wall layers of a microsporangium from outside to inside are:
questions.explanation: The microsporangium wall has epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and innermost tapetum.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Dehiscence of the anther to release pollen is aided by:
questions.explanation: Epidermis, endothecium and middle layers protect the sporangium and facilitate anther dehiscence.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The tapetum of the anther:
questions.explanation: Tapetal cells provide nutrition to developing microspores/pollen grains.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The centrally located cells in a young microsporangium are called:
questions.explanation: Sporogenous tissue occupies the centre and gives rise to microspore mother cells.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Microsporogenesis is:
questions.option_b: Formation of microspores from PMC by meiosis
questions.option_d: Development of embryo sac from nucellus
questions.explanation: Microsporogenesis is meiotic formation of microspores from the pollen mother cell.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Immediately after meiosis in microsporogenesis, microspores are arranged as:
questions.option_b: A microspore tetrad of four cells
questions.explanation: Each PMC produces four microspores grouped as a tetrad.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Microspores develop into pollen grains when anthers:
questions.option_c: Lose all sporogenous tissue before meiosis
questions.explanation: Maturation and dehydration of anthers allow microspores to separate and become pollen grains.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pollen grains are released from the anther through:
questions.explanation: Thousands of pollen grains are liberated when the mature anther dehisces.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pollen grains in angiosperms represent the:
questions.explanation: Each pollen grain is the male gametophyte generation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The typical diameter of pollen grains is approximately:
questions.explanation: Most pollen grains are roughly spherical and 25–50 micrometres across.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The exine of pollen grain is composed of:
questions.explanation: Exine contains sporopollenin, an extremely resistant organic substance.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Germ pores on the pollen exine are sites where:
questions.option_a: Sporopollenin is absent and pollen tube emerges
questions.explanation: Germ pores are thin areas lacking sporopollenin through which pollen tubes germinate.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pollen grains are preserved well in fossils due to:
questions.explanation: Resistant sporopollenin allows pollen to persist in fossil records.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The intine of a pollen grain is made of:
questions.explanation: Intine is the inner thin wall composed of cellulose and pectin.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A mature pollen grain at the 2-celled stage contains:
questions.explanation: At 2-celled stage the pollen has a large vegetative cell and a smaller generative cell.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In more than 60% of angiosperms, pollen is shed at:
questions.explanation: Majority of species release pollen with vegetative and generative cells only.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: In the 3-celled pollen stage, the pollen grain contains:
questions.option_a: Vegetative cell and two male gametes
questions.explanation: Before shedding, generative cell may divide to form two male gametes (3-celled pollen).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pollen viability in rice and wheat lasts approximately:
questions.explanation: Cereal pollen loses viability quickly, within about half an hour of release.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Long-term storage of pollen for breeding programmes uses:
questions.explanation: Cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen allows pollen banks similar to seed banks.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The female reproductive part of a flower is:
questions.explanation: Gynoecium, consisting of pistil(s), is the female reproductive whorl.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A gynoecium with a single pistil is termed:
questions.explanation: Monocarpellary gynoecium has one pistil; multicarpellary has more than one.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Fused pistils in a multicarpellary gynoecium are called:
questions.explanation: Syncarpous pistils are united; apocarpous pistils remain free.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The three parts of a pistil are:
questions.explanation: A pistil comprises stigma, style and ovary.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The stigma of a pistil functions as:
questions.option_b: A landing platform for pollen grains
questions.explanation: Pollen lands on the receptive stigma surface during pollination.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Ovules are also called:
questions.explanation: Each ovule is a megasporangium containing the embryo sac.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The stalk attaching an ovule to the placenta is:
questions.explanation: Funicle connects the ovule body to the placenta.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Hilum of an ovule represents:
questions.option_b: Junction between ovule body and funicle
questions.explanation: Hilum is where the ovule body joins the funicle.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The small opening in integuments at the tip of ovule is:
questions.explanation: Micropyle is the opening through which pollen tube enters the ovule.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The basal part of an ovule opposite the micropyle is:
questions.explanation: Chalaza lies at the base of the ovule opposite the micropylar end.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The mass of cells enclosed within ovule integuments is:
questions.explanation: Nucellus is the central tissue of the ovule enclosing the embryo sac.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which of the following typically has many ovules per ovary?
questions.explanation: Watermelon, papaya and orchids have many ovules; wheat, paddy and mango often have one.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Megasporogenesis is:
questions.option_b: Formation of megaspores from MMC by meiosis
questions.option_c: Fusion of male and female gametes
questions.explanation: Megasporogenesis is meiotic production of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The megaspore mother cell (MMC) is typically located in the:
questions.explanation: A single MMC differentiates in the micropylar part of the nucellus.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Embryo sac development from a single functional megaspore is called:
questions.explanation: Monosporic development uses one megaspore to form the female gametophyte.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Early embryo sac development involves:
questions.option_a: Free nuclear divisions without immediate cell wall formation
questions.option_c: Immediate formation of 7 cells after first division
questions.explanation: Mitosis in the embryo sac initially occurs without cytokinesis (free-nuclear stage).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: The egg apparatus at the micropylar end consists of:
questions.option_b: Two synergids and one egg cell
questions.explanation: Egg apparatus comprises two synergids flanking one egg cell.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Filiform apparatus is found in:
questions.explanation: Synergids possess filiform apparatus that guides the pollen tube.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Antipodal cells are located at:
questions.explanation: Three antipodal cells lie at the chalazal end of the mature embryo sac.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: A mature angiosperm embryo sac is:
questions.explanation: Two polar nuclei share the central cell, giving 8 nuclei in 7 cells.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes microsporogenesis from megasporogenesis?
questions.option_a: Both occur by mitosis in anther
questions.option_b: Microsporogenesis forms microspores in anther; megasporogenesis forms megaspores in ovule
questions.explanation: Microsporogenesis is in anther microsporangia; megasporogenesis in ovule nucellus.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Pollination is defined as:
questions.option_a: Fusion of gametes in embryo sac
questions.option_b: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.explanation: Pollination is pollen transfer from anther to stigma of a pistil.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Autogamy refers to pollination:
questions.explanation: Autogamy is self-pollination within the same flower.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Plants like Viola and Oxalis produce both:
questions.explanation: These plants have open chasmogamous and closed cleistogamous flowers.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Geitonogamy involves pollen transfer:
questions.option_a: From anther to stigma of another flower on the same plant
questions.option_b: From anther to stigma of a different plant only
questions.explanation: Geitonogamy is pollen transfer between flowers of the same plant.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.question: Xenogamy is:
